content: Theophylline and long-acting beta-2 agonists (LABAs) are both bronchodilators used to manage persistent asthma symptoms, including nocturnal asthma. These two drug classes differ in their mechanisms of action and side effect profiles. This study aimed to compare the efficacy, safety, and side effects of LABAs and theophylline in the maintenance treatment of asthma in adults and adolescents. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared oral sustained-release or dose-adjusted theophylline with inhaled LABAs. A total of 13 studies involving 1,344 participants met the inclusion criteria. The quality of the studies varied. The most recent search for relevant studies was conducted in November 2007. The results showed no significant difference between salmeterol (a LABA) and theophylline in terms of predicted forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) (mean difference: 6.5%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.84 to 13.83). However, salmeterol significantly improved morning peak expiratory flow (PEF) by an average of 16.71 L/min (95% CI: 8.91 to 24.51) and evening PEF by an average of 15.58 L/min (95% CI: 8.33 to 22.83) compared to theophylline. Additionally, salmeterol reduced the need for rescue medication. Formoterol, another LABA, was evaluated in two studies and was found to be as effective as theophylline. Bitolterol, a less commonly studied LABA, was reported in one study to be less effective than theophylline. Participants using salmeterol experienced fewer adverse events compared to those taking theophylline. The relative risk (RR) of adverse events in parallel studies was 0.44 (95% CI: 0.30 to 0.63), with a risk difference of -0.11 (95% CI: -0.16 to -0.07). The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one adverse event was 9 (95% CI: 6 to 14). Specifically, there were significant reductions in central nervous system (CNS) adverse events (RR: 0.50; 95% CI: 0.29 to 0.86; risk difference: -0.07; 95% CI: -0.12 to -0.02; NNT: 14; 95% CI: 8 to 50) and gastrointestinal adverse events (RR: 0.30; 95% CI: 0.17 to 0.55; risk difference: -0.11; 95% CI: -0.16 to -0.06; NNT: 9; 95% CI: 6 to 16). In conclusion, LABAs, particularly salmeterol, are more effective than theophylline in improving morning and evening PEF, although there is no significant difference in their effect on FEV1. Salmeterol also reduces the need for short-acting beta-2 agonists during both daytime and nighttime. Furthermore, LABAs (salmeterol and formoterol) are associated with fewer adverse events compared to theophylline.
